claims.text: As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films and nanoribbons have a nanocrystalline microstructure.
As-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films and nanoribbons contain significant residual stress.
A high density of nanoscale grain boundaries governs the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in these low-dimensional alloys.
Residual stress fields govern the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis in these low-dimensional alloys.
Nanoscale grain boundaries and residual stress promote heterogeneous magnetic-phase nucleation.
Residual stress and nanocrystalline interfaces create spatial inhomogeneity in the magnetic phase transition.
Transition inhomogeneity causes staggered domain nucleation and sluggish phase propagation.
Numerous nanocrystalline interfaces impede heat transfer and slow temperature equilibration during cycling.
Slower temperature equilibration broadens the observed hysteresis.
The as-deposited films and nanoribbons exhibit broad hysteresis.
The as-deposited films and nanoribbons have a diminished magnetocaloric response relative to reported bulk specimens.
Post-deposition annealing below the phase-decomposition limit will partially relieve residual stress.
Post-deposition annealing below the phase-decomposition limit will moderately increase grain size.
Stress relief and grain coarsening will reduce spatial transition gradients.
Annealed samples will exhibit narrower magnetic hysteresis than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealed samples will exhibit a magnetocaloric response more similar to bulk behavior than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing may slightly reduce the overall magnetic entropy change by altering the phase-transition distribution.
Heat-transfer rates in the thin-film or nanoribbon geometry limit the usable magnetic-cooling cycle frequency.
The proposed behavior is restricted to low-applied-field cooling cycles near the intrinsic magnetic transition temperature.
Annealing above the decomposition or unwanted-transformation threshold falls outside the hypothesis.
